definitions.type: coordinate differentiation and Euclidean notation convention on the given open domain
definitions.definition: On ℝ^n and ℝ^m use the standard Euclidean inner product v·w=∑_k v_k w_k and norm |v|=(v·v)^(1/2). Spatial Lebesgue measure dx is the product of the n ordinary one-dimensional Lebesgue measures in the standard coordinates. For any function on ℝ^n×(0,∞), ∂_{x_j} means its componentwise derivative in spatial coordinate j (1≤j≤n), and ∂_t its componentwise time derivative, where these derivatives exist. In particular u_t=∂_t u, u_tt=∂_t(∂_t u), and ∂_{x_jx_j}u=∂_{x_j}(∂_{x_j}u). For scalar functions the same conventions apply. D_xu denotes the matrix with columns ∂_{x_j}u, and its squared Frobenius norm is ∑_{j=1}^n |∂_{x_j}u|². Smooth means derivatives of every finite order exist and are continuous on the stated open domain. An integral without a displayed measure is the Lebesgue integral; integrable means measurable with finite integral of the absolute value (or norm).

If f is ContDiffAt K k at z and minSmoothness K 2≤k, then its second Fréchet derivative is symmetric at z: for every v,w∈V, (D(Df)(z)v)w=(D(Df)(z)w)v. output.statement: For all x∈ℝ^n and t>0, u(x,t)·u_t(x,t)=0 and u_t(x,t)·(u_tt(x,t)−Δ_xu(x,t))=0. Any real scalar a satisfying u_tt−Δ_xu=a u at that point equals ∑_{j=1}^n |∂_{x_j}u|²−|u_t|². The density e is smooth on ℝ^n×(0,∞), the mixed derivatives satisfy ∂_t∂_{x_j}u=∂_{x_j}u_t for every 1≤j≤n, and e_t(x,t)=2u_t(x,t)·u_tt(x,t)+2∑_{j=1}^n ∂_{x_j}u(x,t)·∂_{x_j}u_t(x,t). In particular this displayed e_t is continuous.

argument.text: Fix x∈ℝ^n and t>0, and let j be any spatial index with 1≤j≤n when considering a spatial derivative. For any use of a source requiring a curve on all ℝ, extend the time curve by zero at nonpositive times. This extension agrees on a neighborhood of every positive time, so its derivatives there are unchanged by the definition of derivative. By H002 all the coordinate curves and derivatives used here are differentiable near this interior point. H004 gives u(x,r)·u(x,r)=1 for r near t. Apply M007 over ℝ with both curves r↦u(x,r) and both derivatives u_t(x,t). The derivative of the constant right side is zero, while that of the left side is 2u(x,t)·u_t(x,t). Thus u·u_t=0 at (x,t). The same argument along any spatial coordinate gives u·∂_{x_j}u=0. These identities hold throughout the open domain.

produces.statement: Throughout ℝ^n×(0,∞), u·u_t=0 and u·∂_{x_ℓ}u=0 for every spatial index 1≤ℓ≤n.

argument.text: Choose a from H005 at (x,t). Using F001, u_t·(u_tt−Δ_xu)=u_t·(a u)=a(u_t·u)=0, without differentiating a. For completeness retain the explicit equation from the supplied proof. Differentiate the identities u·u_t=0 and u·∂_{x_j}u=0 once more along their respective coordinate curves. M007 gives u·u_tt=−|u_t|² and u·∂_{x_jx_j}u=−|∂_{x_j}u|². Dotting u_tt−Δ_xu=a u with u and using H004 gives a=∑_j|∂_{x_j}u|²−|u_t|². The same algebra applies to every scalar satisfying the normality equation, not just the chosen witness.

produces.statement: At the arbitrary (x,t), u_t·(u_tt−Δ_xu)=0, and for every α∈ℝ, if u_tt−Δ_xu=αu then α=∑_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u|²−|u_t|².

argument.text: By H002, derivatives of every order are continuous; finite inner products and finite sums of their components are smooth, so e is smooth. To identify its time derivative, apply M008 over ℝ to u locally at (x,t), with order 2. One may extend u arbitrarily outside the open domain: all derivative statements are local and the point has a neighborhood wholly in the domain. Evaluate symmetry on the time direction and the jth spatial coordinate direction. These evaluations of the second Fréchet derivative are respectively ∂_t∂_{x_j}u and ∂_{x_j}u_t, hence they agree. Apply M007 to the time curves u_t and u_t, and to ∂_{x_j}u and itself for each index; differentiating the finite sum defining e now gives e_t=2u_t·u_tt+2∑_j∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t. It is continuous by H002. F001 and F002 and these identities hold for arbitrary x,t; universal introduction proves the full output.
